newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Euro-bourse Easdaq says plans index by year-end.
newsitem.headline: Euro-bourse Easdaq says plans index by year-end.

text.p: Pan-European new growth stock market EASDAQ said on Thursday it expected to introduce a market index by the end of the year.
"A London-based player has already expressed interest in launching an index (for EASDAQ)," the bourse's head of admissions Erik Hallmann told a news conference in Amsterdam.
Launching an index earlier had seemed premature, he added.

EASDAQ (European Association of Securities Dealers Automated Quotation) representatives are touring a string of European cities this month to drum up business for the fledgling exchange, which went live last November.
Thursday's roadshow in Amsterdam for 80 prospective listings and members will be followed by similar presentations in Milan, Stuttgart, Rome, Lausanne, and Frankfurt.
The exchange, which currently lists eight companies with total market capitalisation of $1.28 billion and is set to double this number by the summer, has yet to quote its first Dutch stock.
However, Hallmann said that EASDAQ had received an application for listing from an unnamed Dutch information technology firm and was in pre-application talks with several other Dutch companies.
"ING Barings and MeesPierson in the Netherlands are EASDAQ members and we have seen quite a bit of Dutch interest in terms of pre-application talks," Hallmann said.

Despite its stated aim of listing young, high-growth companies, EASDAQ was not in competition with small-cap exchanges such as Amsterdam's recently launched New Market Amsterdam (NMAX), Hallmann stressed.
"We are an integrated, supranational market, catering for a different quality of company... the new markets are more domestic," he said.

NMAX forms part of Euro.NM, a cooperative venture with Paris, Brussels and Frankfurt to trade small-company stocks, which like EASDAQ models itself on NASDAQ, the U.S. based automated quotation system.

EASDAQ's added value lay in its supranational focus on sectors, enabling investors to compare companies across countries based on research available from smaller, specialist securities houses, Hallmann said.
EASDAQ's disclosure requirements are stiffer than those generally required by national exchanges, reflecting the rapid growth of its component stocks.

It requires quarterly earnings reports from its participant stocks rather than the more customary half-year performance figures, and financial information must be presented in accordance with U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) or International Accounting Standards (IAS).
So far EASDAQ stocks all come from the high-technology, pharmaceuticals and biotechnology sectors, but the listing of British carrier Debonair will extend the bourse's scope into civil aviation.
Luton-based Debonair started up in 1996 and has since built up a series of regional European hubs in Copenhagen, Munich and Barcelona. It is expected to quote on EASDAQ around July.
Other imminent newcomers to listing include an unnamed British telecoms company with Dutch links, an Austrian-based information technology company and an Israeli pharmaceuticals firm, he said.
Companies need not show a minimum level of profitability to be admitted to listing, but they must have market capitalisation of $50 million or more.

Applicants must also have a sponsor in the form of an EASDAQ member institution to act as an advisor. Once listed, the stock must have a minimum of two market makers, although the majority of companies currently listed have around seven.
-- Lien van der Leij, Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000
